problems.title: Monty Hall
problems.statement: Standard rules (the host knows and always opens a goat door, then offers a switch).

parts.prompt: If the host opens a random other door and it happens to show a goat?

problems.title: Two children
problems.statement: A family with two children (independent, ½ each).

parts.prompt: P(two boys | at least one boy)?
P(two boys | at least one boy born on Tuesday)?
P(two boys | the older is a boy)?

problems.title: Biased coin
problems.statement: A bag holds one fair coin and one double-headed coin. Pick one at random and flip it.

parts.prompt: P(next flip heads | 3 heads so far)?

problems.title: Two tests
problems.statement: The medical test repeated independently; both positive.

problems.title: Urn
problems.statement: An urn has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Draw two without replacement.

parts.prompt: P(second is red | first is red)?
P(first is red | second is red)?

problems.solution: 2/4 = ½; by symmetry of positions, also ½.

problems.title: Prosecutor
problems.statement: A DNA match probability of 1 in a million for a random person; a city of 5 million; no other evidence.

parts.prompt: Expected innocent matches in the city?
P(the matched suspect is guilty), assuming exactly one culprit in the city?

problems.solution: About 1/6. P(match | innocent) is not P(innocent | match).

problems.title: Sequential evidence
problems.statement: A trader's edge: you think there's a 30% chance a strategy is real (real strategies win 55% of trades; fake ones 50%). It wins 60 of 100 trades.
hints: Odds form with binomial likelihoods (the C(100, 60) cancels).
problems.solution: LR ≈ 4.5, so posterior odds 0.3/0.7 × 4.5 ≈ 1.93, P(real) ≈ 0.66. Sixty wins in a hundred is real evidence, but far from proof: the two hypotheses predict overlapping results at n = 100.
